```{r}
library(dplyr)

immune_obj <- readRDS("../../results/rds/immune_obj.rds")
T_obj <- readRDS("../../results/02.Immune/T_obj.rds")

count_tbl <- function(x) {
	out <- as.data.frame(table(x), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
	colnames(out) <- c("Class", "Cells")
	out <- out %>% arrange(desc(Cells))
	out$Share <- sprintf("%.1f%%", out$Cells / sum(out$Cells) * 100)
	out
}

immune_cell_tbl <- count_tbl(immune_obj$Cell_Type_2)
immune_condition_tbl <- count_tbl(immune_obj$Condition)
t_lineage_tbl <- count_tbl(T_obj$Cell_Type_2)
t_condition_tbl <- count_tbl(T_obj$Condition)

immune_cells <- ncol(immune_obj)
t_cells <- ncol(T_obj)
``` 

## Overview

This report summarizes the immune-cell functional analysis implemented in `code/02.Immune.R`. The analysis begins from the immune subset, performs differential expression for each annotated immune cell type across conditions, follows that with GO enrichment and selected GSEA analyses, and then focuses on T-cell state projection and checkpoint-related programs.

The immune subset contains `r immune_cells` cells. The major immune lineages and states are distributed as follows:

`r knitr::kable(immune_cell_tbl, align = c("l", "r", "r"))`

The T-cell subset used for atlas projection contains `r t_cells` cells and resolves the expected CD4, CD8, Treg, cycling, and related lineage labels:

`r knitr::kable(t_lineage_tbl, align = c("l", "r", "r"))`

The condition balance is preserved in both the full immune compartment and the T-cell subset, which is important for downstream comparison of Capsaicin and 6OHDA against CTRL.

`r knitr::kable(immune_condition_tbl, align = c("l", "r", "r"))`

`r knitr::kable(t_condition_tbl, align = c("l", "r", "r"))`

## Cell-Type Differential Expression

The core analysis loop in `code/02.Immune.R` runs `FindMarkers` separately within each immune cell type, comparing Capsaicin vs CTRL and 6OHDA vs CTRL. This design keeps cell-state-specific responses intact and avoids mixing signals from unrelated lineages.

Across both perturbations, the volcano plots show that the strongest signals are not uniform across the immune landscape. Instead, each cell type contributes its own set of up- and down-regulated genes, with clear enrichment of stress-response, interferon/inflammatory, migration, and activation programs in the more responsive compartments.

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Volcano.Capsaicin_vs_CTRL.png" width="100%">

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Volcano.6OHDA_vs_CTRL.png" width="100%">

### Representative GO enrichment by cell type

The GO dot plots show that Capsaicin and 6OHDA drive cell-type-specific biological processes rather than a single shared immune-wide response. Representative examples include CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, Tregs, cDC, monocytes/macrophages, and neutrophils.

For Capsaicin, the GO enrichment plots emphasize immune activation, cellular response to stress, and regulation of effector programs across T-cell and myeloid compartments.

<img src="assets/02.Immune/GO_Capsaicin/Dot.GO_Capsaicin_vs_CTRL_Neutrophil_UP.png" width="100%">

## T-Cell Atlas Projection

To resolve T-cell functional states, the T-cell subset is projected onto the ProjecTILs mouse TIL atlas. This step provides an external atlas-based annotation of the T-cell compartment and places the BLCA immune cells into a familiar CD4/CD8/Treg functional framework.

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Projection_of_T_cells.png" width="100%">

The radar plot summarizes the projected state composition and makes the dominant functional axes easy to compare across the atlas reference and the query data.

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Radar.T.Projection.png" width="100%">

The condition-wise fraction plots show how the projected T-cell states are redistributed across CTRL, Capsaicin, and 6OHDA.

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Barplot.T_subtype.Condition.png" width="100%">

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Boxplot.Fraction.T_subtype.png" width="100%">

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Boxplot.Fraction.T_subtype.Merge.png" width="100%">

The Roe heatmap provides a compact summary of whether the projected states are enriched or depleted in particular conditions.

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Heatmap.Roe.T_state.Condition.png" width="100%">

The marker plots support the ProjecTILs state calls. They show the expected separation between suppressive/regulatory features, cytotoxic programs, and exhaustion-associated checkpoint markers.

## T-Cell Program Signatures

The signature-level analysis expands the marker view into broader T-cell programs. These plots are useful for separating suppressive/regulatory tendencies from cytotoxicity and exhaustion-like states.

<img src="assets/02.Immune/Dot.T_state.Signature.Condition.png" width="100%">

The signature plots reinforce the same conclusion at both the pooled and state-specific levels: condition effects on T cells are organized around immune activation, suppression, and exhaustion-related programs rather than a single uniform shift.

## Selected GSEA Results

The Capsaicin GSEA plots provide a more focused view of pathway-level changes in selected T-cell and myeloid subsets. In the report outputs, T_CD4 and neutrophils show especially readable enrichment patterns.

## Takeaway

The immune analysis shows that Capsaicin and 6OHDA drive cell-type-specific transcriptional changes across the immune compartment, with the strongest and most interpretable effects in T cells and neutrophils. The cross-condition comparison indicates that some pathways are broadly shared while others are distinctly perturbation-specific. The ProjecTILs projection further resolves the T-cell compartment into recognizable functional states, and the marker/signature plots support the conclusion that immune activation, suppression, and exhaustion-related programs are all being remodeled in the BLCA microenvironment.
